label: Sun · Jul 26
standfirst: Wall Street heads into the most consequential week of the year — a knife-edge FOMC decision and earnings from four of the Magnificent Seven — with a fragile Iran pause holding after U.S. forces skipped fresh strikes for the first time in two weeks.
marketsNote: Weekend leaves Friday's split tape on the board: the Dow rose 0.46% to 51,947 and the S&P 500 was flat while the Nasdaq fell 0.64% on AI-capex nerves. Crude tumbled — WTI -3.54% to $88.93, Brent -3.8% to $96.88 — as the Iran conflict cooled, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 4.68% into a pivotal week.

lead.headline: Markets brace for a make-or-break week: FOMC on Wednesday collides with Big Tech's biggest earnings stretch
body: Wall Street enters the week facing its densest calendar of the year. The Federal Reserve announces its rate decision Wednesday at the close of the July 28–29 FOMC meeting, and traders remain split: a hold is the base case, but a hot oil-driven inflation impulse has revived hawkish talk, leaving markets to parse the statement's language on energy and financial conditions rather than the rate itself.

Layered on top is a wall of earnings, with Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Apple all due — four of the Magnificent Seven whose AI capital-spending plans will set the tone after Thursday's roughly $800 billion single-day wipeout across the group. Friday offered a preview of the new regime: the Dow climbed on solid non-tech results while the Nasdaq slipped, as investors rewarded execution and punished open-ended AI spend.

banking.lead: American Express disappointed.
banking.text: AXP shares slid about 4.5% Friday despite a solid Q2 profit, after revenue and net interest income came in lighter than Wall Street expected — a rare stumble for the premium-card lender and a caution flag on consumer-credit momentum.

banking.lead: The Fed takes center stage.
banking.text: The July 28–29 FOMC meeting ends Wednesday with a rate call at 2:00 p.m. ET. Markets lean toward a hold, but sticky, oil-fed inflation has narrowed the Fed's options — cut too soon and price fears return; hold too long and rate-sensitive sectors keep compressing.

banking.lead: Dealmaking is booming.
banking.text: Wall Street's investment-banking machine is 'firing on all cylinders,' with a 2026 wave of IPOs, mergers and new debt issuance lifting fee pipelines at Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and peers as bankers gear up for a record M&A supercycle.

banking.lead: Tariffs are now live.
banking.text: President Trump's latest global tariffs — roughly 10% to 12.5% on nearly all U.S. imports from major trading partners — took effect, injecting fresh cost-and-inflation uncertainty into the Fed's calculus and corporate margins alike.

banking.lead: Verizon beat, telecom held up.
banking.text: Verizon topped estimates in its quarterly report, a bright spot among the value names that steadied the Dow even as high-multiple tech absorbed the week's selling.

watch.title: The FOMC verdict
watch.text: The rate decision itself may matter less than the tone. Watch the statement's language on energy prices and inflation, and the first 15 minutes of the bond-market reaction, for whether investors believe the Fed can look through oil-driven inflation — the read-through will steer equities into month-end.

world.text: For the first time in two weeks, U.S. forces did not announce fresh strikes on Iran as of July 25, easing a campaign that had run 13 consecutive nights. Thursday's strikes killed four and damaged Revolutionary Guard facilities before the apparent pause.
Crude retreated sharply — WTI down 3.54% and Brent off 3.8% Friday — as the halt in strikes drained the geopolitical risk premium that had briefly pushed Brent above $100 earlier in the week.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convened his security cabinet ahead of a planned trip to Washington, with the Iran file and regional shipping security topping the agenda.
The Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea remain flashpoints after Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping earlier in the week, keeping energy and freight markets on alert even as strikes paused.
With sweeping U.S. tariffs now in force, trading partners weigh responses, adding a fresh layer of uncertainty to global supply chains and the inflation outlook heading into autumn.

sources: TheStreet; CNBC; Reuters; Bloomberg; Yahoo Finance; Forbes; Washington Post; CNN; The Times of Israel; MarketBeat

label: Sat · Jul 25
standfirst: With oil above $100 and inflation running hot, traders have flipped to pricing a real chance the Fed HIKES next week — a stark reversal from the September-cut consensus — as a Big Tech earnings deluge and the FOMC collide with a fragile pause in the Iran war.
marketsNote: U.S. markets were closed for the weekend, leaving Friday's mixed finish on the board: the Dow up 0.46% and the S&P 500 flat while the Nasdaq slipped 0.64%. All eyes now turn to a pivotal week — the FOMC decision on July 28-29 and results from Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Apple — with the 10-year Treasury yield last at 4.68% and crude having whipsawed around $100 on Middle East risk.

lead.headline: Fed rate-HIKE bets triple into a make-or-break week as oil and inflation upend the cut narrative
body: The story heading into next week has flipped. As recently as mid-July, Wall Street was debating when the Fed would start cutting; by this weekend, traders were seriously pricing a rate INCREASE at the July 28-29 meeting. CME Group's FedWatch tool showed hike odds jumping from just 10.7% on July 15 to 34.7% by July 22, with some trackers putting the probability near 38% by Friday — more than a tripling in barely a week.

The drivers are stacking up. Brent crude vaulted nearly 7% past $100 a barrel and WTI rose 5.3% to about $91 after Houthi attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, reviving inflation fears just as core PCE — the Fed's preferred gauge — sits at 3.4%, its highest since October 2023, with headline PCE at 4.1%, more than double the 2% target. Layered on top is the enormous AI data-center build-out, whose demand for chips and power is itself pushing prices higher. That collision — sticky inflation versus a wobbling, debt-financed AI rally — is what makes the coming week the most consequential of the summer.

banking.lead: The odds of a July rate hike have tripled.
banking.text: CME FedWatch data showed the implied probability of a quarter-point increase at the July 28-29 FOMC climbing from 10.7% on July 15 to 34.7% by July 22, with some readings near 38% by Friday. A week ago the debate was about a September cut; now a hold is the base case and a hike is a live risk.

banking.lead: Inflation is proving stubborn beyond energy.
banking.text: Core PCE rose to 3.4% as of May — the highest since October 2023 — while headline PCE hit 4.1%, more than double the Fed's 2% target. Analysts note the pressure is broad-based, spanning oil, tariffs and AI-hardware costs rather than any single shock, complicating the case for near-term easing.

banking.lead: A Big Tech earnings deluge lands next week.
banking.text: About a third of the S&P 500 reports, headlined by Microsoft, Meta and Amazon and followed by Apple, Visa, Chevron and Coca-Cola. The central question: whether the hyperscalers are generating enough cash to justify soaring AI capital spending, the same anxiety that erased close to $800 billion from the Magnificent Seven on Thursday.

banking.lead: A higher-for-longer Fed threatens the AI trade.
banking.text: Because much of the data-center build-out is debt-financed, any hint that borrowing costs will rise — or simply stay elevated — jeopardizes the leverage underpinning the rally. Strategists warn the market is 'walking on eggshells' after two straight down weeks for the S&P 500.

banking.lead: Sentiment gauges are still flashing caution.
banking.text: Bank of America's Bull & Bear indicator remains at its highest reading since 2021, a contrarian warning sign driven by strong fund inflows and stretched hedge-fund positioning — froth that has historically preceded pullbacks.

banking.lead: Oil's surge is the swing factor for rates.
banking.text: Brent's leap past $100 and WTI's climb to roughly $91 on Red Sea disruptions feed directly into inflation expectations. Rystad Energy sees crude easing toward $70 by Q4 under a 'narrow deal,' but a prolonged conflict could push prices toward $150 by September — a spread that could decide the Fed's next several moves.

watch.title: FOMC decision, July 28-29
watch.lead: The week's marquee event, now with two-sided risk.
watch.text: For the first time this cycle, markets are weighing whether the Fed holds or delivers a surprise hike. Watch the statement and the Chair's tone for how policymakers balance tariff- and oil-driven inflation against a Big Tech complex that is suddenly wobbling. The decision lands mid-week alongside Q2 GDP, fresh inflation data and the heaviest slate of mega-cap earnings of the season.

world.lead: US-Iran strikes appeared to pause, but a new front opened at sea.
world.text: After roughly two weeks and 13-plus consecutive nights of strikes, Washington and Tehran appeared to hold fire this weekend. The relief was undercut by the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi oil tankers on July 23, framing it as a blockade of Saudi shipping and widening the war's economic reach.

Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan and Oman have offered the U.S. and Iran a 10-day truce that would restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and open talks on a longer-term deal. The proposal is the most concrete off-ramp yet, though earlier ceasefires this year collapsed within days.

world.lead: The world's key oil chokepoints are seizing up.
world.text: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell about 31% day-on-day and Bab el-Mandeb dropped 34% as tankers avoided the crossfire. With Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline moving up to 5 million barrels a day and Bab el-Mandeb handling roughly 9 million, the disruption keeps global energy markets on edge.

world.lead: Zelenskyy will meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday.
world.text: The White House confirmed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet President Trump on July 29 to revive stalled peace talks sidelined by the Iran crisis. Trump is also set to meet Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu the same day — which coincides with a memorial for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent Ukraine backer who died this month at 71.

world.lead: Spain declared its first-ever national wildfire emergency.
world.text: As blazes merged near Madrid, Spain invoked a first-of-its-kind national emergency, with thousands evacuated amid a punishing heatwave. France continued deploying water bombers across its western regions as southern Europe's fire season intensified.

sources: CNBC; Reuters; The Motley Fool; Forbes; Yahoo Finance; HNGN; CNN; Al Jazeera; The Defense Post; Business Standard; The Washington Post; Euronews

label: Fri · Jul 24
standfirst: Crude reversed hard and blue chips clawed back as reports emerged that Pakistan, with China's backing, is pushing for fresh U.S.-Iran talks — draining the war premium that had spiked oil 7% a day earlier.
marketsNote: A split, whipsaw finish to a bruising week: the Dow rose 235.60 points to 51,947.25 and the S&P 500 eked out 7,411.98 as falling oil lifted cyclicals, while the Nasdaq slipped 0.6% to 24,975.82 on lingering Big Tech capex angst — Brent sank back near $95 and WTI near $87 as Middle East de-escalation hopes revived.

lead.headline: Oil's war premium drains away as Pakistan floats new U.S.-Iran talks, steadying a rattled Wall Street
body: The day's decisive turn came from the oil pits. After Thursday's 7% surge toward $100 on Houthi tanker strikes and Trump's threats against Iranian infrastructure, crude reversed sharply Friday — Brent tumbling roughly 5.7% back toward $95 and WTI down about 5.6% near $87 — on reports that Pakistan, with Beijing's backing, is quietly pushing for fresh U.S.-Iran negotiations. The easing energy shock let blue-chip cyclicals lead a rebound, lifting the Dow 235.60 points to 51,947.25 and nudging the S&P 500 to a barely-changed 7,411.98.

Technology stayed the sore spot. The Nasdaq slipped 0.6% to 24,975.82 as investors kept punishing hyperscaler spending plans — Intel fell about 4% despite an earnings beat, weighed by heavy capex, and post-IPO SpaceX slid to fresh lows. The net for the week was still red across the major averages, but Friday's stabilization, powered entirely by the geopolitical off-ramp, kept the sell-off from deepening into the weekend.

banking.lead: American Express beat.
banking.text: AmEx closed the day's earnings slate with Q2 profit up 8% to $4.53 a share, topping the Street's ~$4.40 estimate on record cardmember billings and falling delinquencies, and it nudged up its full-year revenue forecast — a clean read on the resilient affluent US consumer.

banking.lead: Morgan Stanley eyes a record.
banking.text: Executives reiterated that the investment-banking pipeline could make 2026 a record year, with M&A and equity-issuance mandates building even as tariff and rate uncertainty churns the tape — a bullish signal for advisory-fee momentum into the second half.

banking.lead: Goldman calls a mega-deal wave.
banking.text: Goldman Sachs is sticking with its forecast of a blockbuster 2026 for M&A, arguing pent-up sponsor demand and a friendlier antitrust posture will unlock large strategic combinations — the kind of dealmaking that drove this quarter's advisory upside.

banking.lead: Bankers pivot to a busy pipeline.
banking.text: After cashing in on a heavy Q2 deal slate, Wall Street bankers are shifting focus to a crowded 2026 backlog; the mid-July megabank results showed trading and investment-banking fees doing the heavy lifting, and firms are staffing up for the follow-through.

banking.lead: Bank stocks steady with the tape.
banking.text: Financials firmed alongside the blue-chip rebound as the retreat in oil eased the stagflation worry that had gripped markets Thursday, letting rate-sensitive lenders and cyclicals recover part of the week's losses.

watch.title: The Iran off-ramp
watch.lead: Watch whether the talks are real.
watch.text: The entire Friday reversal hinges on a diplomatic thread — Pakistan-brokered, China-backed talks that Iran has yet to confirm, even as US strikes entered a 13th night and Tehran rejected an earlier Iraq-relayed ceasefire. With Apollo pegging Iran's sway over roughly 38% of seaborne oil via Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, any breakdown snaps the war premium back into crude and back onto stocks; any real progress extends the relief. Next week's mega-cap tech earnings and Fed signals are the other swing factors.

world.text: President Trump told Axios he is 'considering a massive attack' on Iran and is 'close to making a decision,' as the US carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iranian command centers, drone sites and coastal infrastructure; the WSJ reported he is losing patience with a war that has no clear end.

Countering the escalation, reports say Pakistan — with China's backing — is pushing to convene new US-Iran talks, the development that drove Friday's oil plunge; Iran, however, rejected a separate ceasefire proposal delivered via Iraq's president, leaving the off-ramp unconfirmed.

Trump's latest package of double-digit tariffs — 10% to 12.5% on dozens of major trading partners covering nearly all US imports — went into force Friday, adding a fresh cost-and-inflation variable just as markets try to stabilize.

Apollo data show Iran now influences about 38% of maritime oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb — some 29.5 million of 78.4 million barrels moving daily; Iraqi and Kuwaiti exports have effectively fallen to zero and Saudi Arabia's Red Sea outlet is blocked by Houthi forces.

Initial US jobless claims fell 22,000 to 187,000 for the week ended July 18, with continuing claims down to 1.80 million — a still-tight labor picture that complicates the Fed's path as tariffs and oil swings cloud the inflation outlook.

sources: CNBC; Reuters; Bloomberg; Yahoo Finance; The Motley Fool; Fortune; The Washington Post; U.S. News; Wall Street Journal

label: Thu · Jul 23
standfirst: Stocks tumbled and the Nasdaq lost nearly 2% as oil surged toward $100 on Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers and Tesla cratered 12% on Musk's 'massive capex year' warning.
marketsNote: The selloff was led by megacap tech: the Dow shed 503.69 points to close at 51,714.89, the S&P 500 fell 1.00% to 7,424.24 and the Nasdaq slid 1.86% to 25,212.45, while WTI settled near $90 and Brent near $98 as the 10-year Treasury yield hit an 18-month high.

lead.headline: Oil rockets toward $100 and Big Tech buckles, dragging Wall Street to its worst day of the week
body: U.S. stocks closed sharply lower Thursday as a fresh spike in crude prices collided with disappointing megacap-tech guidance. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.86% to 25,212.45, the S&P 500 lost 1.00% to 7,424.24 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 503.69 points, or 0.96%, to 51,714.89; the small-cap Russell 2000 held up better, down 0.67% to 2,940.02. Brent crude jumped roughly 3.7% to close near $98 a barrel and WTI rose about 3.8% to settle near $90 after Iran-backed Houthi militants attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, reviving fears of a broader supply shock.

The tech damage was concentrated in the megacaps that reported after Wednesday's bell. Tesla plunged 12.38% after Elon Musk told investors 2026 would be a 'massive capex year' devoted to Optimus robots, robotaxis and data centers, while Alphabet slid as investors balked at its swelling capital-spending plans. Rising oil prices fed a bond-market selloff that pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest level in about 18 months, stoking fresh inflation worries and casting doubt on the timing of the Federal Reserve's next rate cut. A stronger-than-expected labor read — initial jobless claims of 187,000 versus a forecast near 210,000 — added to the case for the Fed to stay patient.

banking.lead: Bonds sold off hard.
banking.text: The oil-driven inflation scare triggered a slide in Treasuries, lifting the 10-year yield to roughly an 18-month high and steepening the curve. Higher long-end rates pressured rate-sensitive financials and revived questions about unrealized losses sitting on bank balance sheets.

banking.lead: Rate-cut bets got pushed back.
banking.text: With Brent closing in on $100 and jobless claims coming in at just 187,000, traders trimmed the odds of a near-term Fed cut. A higher-for-longer path complicates net-interest-margin math for lenders heading into the back half of the year.

banking.lead: Wall Street's dealmaking engine is still humming.
banking.text: The backdrop for the big banks remains strong after a Q2 earnings season in which trading and investment-banking revenue surged across the bulge bracket, with Goldman Sachs and peers citing a revival in M&A and capital-markets activity. Thursday's volatility spike is a double-edged sword: good for trading desks, potentially chilling for the deal pipeline if it persists.

banking.lead: Financial stocks tracked the tape lower.
banking.text: Banks, insurers and asset managers followed the broad risk-off move, though small caps' relative resilience cushioned some regional names. Energy and defense were among the few sectors catching a bid as crude and geopolitical premia climbed.

banking.lead: Megacap capex is the market's new fault line.
banking.text: The Tesla and Alphabet reactions underscore how sensitive equity valuations have become to AI- and hardware-related spending. Investors are increasingly demanding a clearer line of sight to returns on the hundreds of billions the megacaps are pouring into data centers and robotics.

watch.title: Does Brent break $100?
watch.lead: The oil tape now sets the tone.
watch.text: A sustained move above $100 a barrel would harden the inflation narrative, keep the Fed on hold and pressure equities further; a de-escalation in the Red Sea could just as quickly unwind the premium. Watch Friday's earnings from Intel, T-Mobile US and Lockheed Martin, plus any move in the 10-year yield, for the next read on how far the risk-off mood runs.

world.lead: Houthis struck Saudi tankers in the Red Sea.
world.text: Iran-backed Houthi militants attacked two Saudi oil tankers crossing the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, setting a fire at the bow of the vessel Encelia — crew unharmed — and claiming to have forced roughly 10 ships to retreat. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged the Houthis to 'stay out of it,' saying they had been 'snookered' by Tehran.

President Trump threatened to destroy Iranian bridges and power plants after attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, and U.S. Central Command carried out overnight B-1 bomber strikes on drone-storage and air-defense sites — a first for this phase. Iran's IRGC said it struck U.S. targets in Kuwait and Jordan, sending Brent up some $13 on the week.

world.lead: Israel and Lebanon set a new round of talks.
world.text: Lebanese officials said the next U.S.-brokered talks with Israel are scheduled for August 4 in Italy, a modest sign of diplomatic momentum even as the wider region simmers.

world.lead: The EU tightened the screws on Russia.
world.text: EU diplomats agreed on a 21st sanctions package targeting 94 Russian financial institutions, the Moscow stock exchange and shadow-fleet vessels, while Ukraine agreed to export drones to the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program.

world.lead: House Republicans passed a war-tinged budget.
world.text: The House narrowly approved a $95 billion budget plan by 216-214, including $73 billion in Iran war funding, and a defense authorization bill cleared with six Democratic crossovers as Washington aligned behind the escalating campaign.

sources: CNBC; Yahoo Finance; Forbes; Reuters; Bloomberg; The Washington Post; The National; Just Security; Wikipedia Current Events

label: Wed · Jul 22
standfirst: Alphabet blew past estimates with cloud revenue up 82% while Tesla's profit cratered on vanishing EV credits, splitting the verdict as Big Tech earnings opened after a tech-led rally.
marketsNote: Stocks closed broadly higher, led by large-cap tech, as investors positioned ahead of the first heavyweight earnings of the season; crude stayed bid above $92 on Strait of Hormuz tensions.

lead.headline: Big Tech earnings open with a split verdict: Alphabet crushes it, Tesla's profit collapses
body: The Nasdaq led Wall Street higher on Wednesday, rising 1.29% while the S&P 500 added 0.89% and the Dow gained 0.74%, as traders rotated into growth names ahead of the quarter's marquee earnings. The rally set the stage for an after-the-bell reckoning that delivered two very different stories.

Alphabet blew past expectations, posting $119.8 billion in revenue (up 24%) and diluted EPS of $9.11, with Google Cloud revenue surging 82% to $24.8 billion and cloud operating income jumping to $8.8 billion from $2.8 billion a year earlier. The company also disclosed $44.9 billion of quarterly capex, a signal that the AI-infrastructure arms race is still accelerating.

Tesla told the opposite tale: record revenue of $28.24 billion (up 26%) beat forecasts, but non-GAAP EPS of $0.33 badly missed the $0.53 consensus and fell 18% year over year, as operating margin sank to 1.4% from 4.1% and regulatory-credit income collapsed 67% to $146 million after federal EV incentives lapsed. Free cash flow turned negative for the first time since early 2024.

banking.lead: Wall Street's deal machine is running hot.
banking.text: Investment-banking fees at the six largest U.S. banks jumped roughly 45% year over year in Q2, with Morgan Stanley posting the biggest percentage gain. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said the advisory backlog hit its highest level in five years.

banking.lead: The IPO window is wide open.
banking.text: U.S. IPOs raised a record $104.8 billion in the second quarter, powered by SpaceX's historic listing. Bankers are already eyeing potential mega-listings from Anthropic and OpenAI, each floated at trillion-dollar valuations.

banking.lead: M&A volumes are back above trend.
banking.text: Global announced deal volumes have topped $3 trillion year to date, up more than 40% from a year ago, with technology and AI names dominating alongside strength in healthcare, utilities and energy.

banking.lead: Analysts see a super-cycle, not a spike.
banking.text: Morningstar expects the investment-banking upswing to run without material contraction until 2028 or later, as JPMorgan, Citi and Bank of America executives all pointed to robust, broad-based capital-markets pipelines.

banking.lead: Regional banks eye the Fed.
banking.text: Smaller lenders are in focus ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting, with investors weighing the path of rates against still-elevated deposit costs and commercial-real-estate exposure.

watch.title: The rest of Big Tech
watch.lead: One night down, the heavyweights still to come.
watch.text: With Alphabet and Tesla setting the tone, attention turns to Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon in the days ahead, and to whether their AI-capex guidance justifies this year's valuations. Layered on top is next week's Fed meeting, which will test how much rate-cut optimism is already priced in.

world.text: U.S. forces carried out an 11th straight night of strikes on Iranian military infrastructure, with Central Command citing threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Crude pushed above $92 a barrel on the disruption.

world.lead: Trump greenlights a Saudi nuclear pact.
world.text: The president approved a 30-year civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that could permit uranium enrichment on Saudi soil and positions U.S. firms to lead the buildout while shutting out foreign rivals.
President Zelenskyy replaced military commander Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi after nationwide protests over defense strategy, amid tensions over reform priorities and mobilization.
Tens of thousands protested in New Delhi over exam-corruption allegations, drawing opposition support and demands for the education minister's resignation.
Andy Burnham began his tenure as UK prime minister, naming John Healey chancellor and announcing a cut to VAT on energy costs.

sources: CNBC; Reuters; Bloomberg; Yahoo Finance; Qz; Electrek; 9to5Google; Investing.com; The Globe and Mail; KuCoin; 10 Things Global News

label: Tue · Jul 21
standfirst: Wall Street closed the best bank-earnings season in history even as fresh U.S. strikes on Iran and a Houthi blockade threat rattled markets. The stories that matter most to you, below.
marketsNote: Roughly 86% of S&P 500 companies have beaten expectations so far this season. U.S. gasoline averaged $3.99 a gallon amid the Iran conflict.

lead.headline: Big banks post the strongest quarter in history — JPMorgan books the largest profit ever
body: All five major U.S. banks blew past estimates in the second quarter, powered by a trading boom and blockbuster deal activity — most notably the $85.7 billion SpaceX IPO, which alone generated roughly $500 million in underwriting fees split across the group. JPMorgan led with $21.2 billion in net income, the single largest quarterly profit in U.S. banking history, on revenue of $58.0 billion, up 27%.

CEO Jamie Dimon still struck a cautious note, warning of geopolitical instability, persistent inflation, and swelling sovereign debt. Goldman Sachs delivered the biggest surprise — earnings of $20.98 a share against a $14.47 estimate. Wells Fargo reported its first full quarter free of the Fed's multi-year asset cap.

banking.lead: Housing Act becomes law.
banking.text: Congress enacted the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Title IX delivers community-banking reforms: expanded reciprocal deposit exceptions, a two-year capital phase-in for de novo banks, and 18-month exam cycles for banks up to $6 billion in assets.

banking.lead: Banks eye Fiserv's STAR network.
banking.text: JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and PNC reportedly held preliminary talks to acquire Fiserv's STAR debit network (115 million cardholders) — a way to sidestep Durbin interchange caps, but expect heavy scrutiny.

banking.lead: The Fed launches a sweeping review.
banking.text: Chair Kevin Warsh named 15 outside advisers across five task forces spanning communications, the balance sheet, and inflation frameworks. Panelists include Marc Andreessen and Raghuram Rajan; recommendations due by year-end.

banking.lead: Circle, Sony, and Klarna go bank.
banking.text: Circle won approval for a national trust bank offering digital-asset custody. Sony gained conditional approval for a trust bank planning dollar-backed stablecoins, and Klarna applied for a Utah industrial bank charter.

banking.lead: CFPB staffing cuts frozen.
banking.text: A federal judge temporarily blocked the bureau's workforce reduction until 60 days after a Senate-confirmed director takes office.

banking.lead: SWIFT tests a blockchain ledger.
banking.text: SWIFT launched a pilot with 17 global banks, testing 24/7 cross-border payments using tokenized deposits.

watch.title: The Fed's next move
watch.text: The FOMC meets July 28–29 with rates held at 3.50%–3.75%. Inflation is running hot — PCE at 3.6% and CPI up to 4.2% in May — and the room is split: nine of 18 officials penciled in at least one 2026 hike in June, while others still see cuts. No new projections accompany this meeting, so the statement language is the tell.

world.text: U.S. Central Command carried out a ninth consecutive night of strikes on Iranian military targets under Operation Epic Fury. Three American service members were killed in recent days. Yemen's Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Russia launched one of its largest ballistic-missile barrages against Ukraine since the 2022 invasion began.
Venezuela's twin-earthquake death toll rose to 5,208. A 7.3-magnitude quake struck Mexico's southern coast; a 5.5 quake in Peru's Andes killed at least six.
Spain edged Argentina 1–0 in the final, with President Trump, Canada's PM Carney, and Mexico's President Sheinbaum in attendance.
Tesla, Alphabet, and Intel headline the coming week.

sources: CNBC & TheStreet market recaps; TechTimes / Intellectia Q2 bank earnings; Bankeration Banking Roundup; Forbes Fed Meeting Tracker; Everything Briefing global roundup.
